                                                INTRODUCTION

         Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro (“EMM” or the “Company”) respectfully

submits this Post-Hearing Reply Brief (“Reply Brief”) in response to the initial post-hearing briefs

of the Staff (“Staff”) of the Missouri Public Service Commission (“Commission”), the Office of

the Public Counsel (“OPC”), Google LLC (“Google”), Velvet Tech Services, LLC (“Velvet

Tech”), and the Midwest Energy Consumers Group (“MECG”). 1 This Reply Brief follows the

organization of the Initial Brief. 2

         None of the other parties’ initial briefs disputes the crucial context leading to this rate case:

The Company’s total rates decreased by 2.2% from 2017 through October 2025, while the rates of

electric utilities in peer states increased by an average of 18.8% and inflation increased by

approximately 29%. 3 In 2025, the Company had the 16th lowest average residential bill among

the 100 largest investor-owned electric utilities with bundled sales. 4 The Company now requests

an increase of $88.9 million, which is less than 10% and amounts to a cumulative change of about

9.6% since the end of 2017. 5 The investments at issue in this case keep service safe and reliable,

and the requested return at issue allows the Company to finance them.

          Under well-established Missouri ratemaking principles and law, the Commission must set

just and reasonable rates, and the Company bears the burden of proving that its proposed rates

meet that standard. 6 Setting just and reasonable rates “involves a balancing of the investor and the

consumer interests.” 7 As detailed in the Initial Brief and below, the Company has amply carried

its burden of proof for the requested increase in this rate case, which balances investor and

consumer interests, is just and reasonable, and is supported by substantial evidence on the record

as a whole.

         In addition to the six stipulations and agreements filed in October and the parties’ Joint

List of Status of Issues, the parties’ initial briefs further narrow this case considerably. 8 Four of

the agreements drew only two objections between them, each to a single term. Staff asks the

Commission to adopt the Partial Stipulation, the Pensions Stipulation, the Non-C&I Rate Design

Stipulation, and the Programs Stipulation “in their entirety, without modification.” 9 OPC does not

oppose those four agreements except on the customer charge waiver program it seeks under Issue

16.E. 10 MECG objects to one term of the Partial Stipulation—the retirement dates for Iatan Unit

1 and La Cygne Unit 2 under Issue 17.A. 11 Google does not oppose any of the four agreements,

and Velvet Tech’s brief addresses only the LLPS issues. 12 Renew Missouri signed the Programs

Stipulation, does not oppose the Partial Stipulation, and lists no objection to any agreement on the

Joint Status List.13 The Commission should approve those four agreements as filed.

dispute the LLPS revenue reflected in rates (Issue 3.A), the LLPS tariff (Issue 31), the FAC terms

(Issues 22, 23, and 25), and the earnings review (Issue 37).                    Google defends the revenue

adjustment, the FAC terms, and the earnings review. 14 Velvet Tech asks the Commission to “make

minimal changes to Schedule LLPS in this case” and does not ask the Commission to reject the

agreement. 15 MECG supports the $60 million revenue adjustment. 16

        This is a transitional case for Schedule LLPS. As Mr. Lutz told the Chair, it is “a

transitional case where we do not have a customer present in the test year to inform rate making.” 17

The LLPS Stipulation therefore sets rates on the LLPS revenue that was known and measurable at

the true-up, and it leaves later growth subject to the annual earnings review process. Staff’s

alternatives rest on estimates of load that had not arrived by the true-up. Asked by the Chair

whether “in the next case, we would know for sure what the revenue requirement and billing

determinants for the large load customers are,” Mr. Lutz agreed: “For Metro, in the next filing, we

will have large load customers present. We will have costs.” 18 The Commission should decide

those questions on that record.

                              The $60 Million Annualizes the June 2026 Bills

         While Mr. Ives did use the word “negotiated” at the on-the-record presentation, as Staff

attempts to mischaracterize, 34 the full exchange shows what was negotiated. When Staff’s counsel

2026 amount.” 35 He explained that the Company “looked at the June revenues billed and the

billing determinants, which was the last month of the true-up period, and annualized that.” 36 The

only adjustment from the Company’s earlier $43 million was the one Dr. Berry identified, which

applies the energy charges on top of the minimum demand of 80% of contract capacity. 37 Both

figures were calculated under the existing tariff at the rates in effect in June 2026. 38 The only

element the signatories negotiated was the rounding of Dr. Berry’s calculation, and Staff’s

objection “did not identify an error” in that calculation. 39

         The only figure any witness called a plug was Staff’s own. Ms. Lange testified that Staff

“had to present” its Customer A revenue “for true-up as a true-up plug, just in order to kind of

make things make sense.” 40

customers, “Staff may perform an individualized annualization based on the customer’s specific

circumstances.” 41 An annualization of the last month of the true-up period at the tariff’s minimum

demand is exactly that.
